title: Scalar-extended infinitesimal points and conjugation for affine groups
statement:
Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field] and $J$ an affine $k$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], with identity $e$. Put $L_J=T_{J/k,e}$ [def-sc-scheme-tangent-space]. Then $L_J$ is a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space. For every commutative $k$-algebra $R$, write $R[\delta]=R[T]/(T^2)$, with $\delta$ the class of $T$ [def-sc-dual-numbers], and let $p_R:R[\delta]\to R$ set $\delta=0$. There are canonical bijections
$$E_{J,R}:L_J\otimes_k R\xrightarrow{\sim}\ker(J(p_R):J(R[\delta])\to J(R)),$$
where the kernel is the set of points reducing to the identity. For $R=k$ this is the defining identification of tangent vectors. They satisfy
$$E_{J,R}(u+v)=E_{J,R}(u)E_{J,R}(v),\quad E_{J,R}(0)=e,\quad E_{J,R}(-u)=E_{J,R}(u)^{-1}.$$
For $a\in R$, applying $J$ to $R[\delta]\to R[\delta]$, $\delta\mapsto a\delta$, sends $E_{J,R}(u)$ to $E_{J,R}(au)$. The bijections are natural under homomorphisms of commutative $k$-algebras $R\to R'$ and homomorphisms of affine finite-type $k$-group schemes $f:J\to J'$: their tangent maps $\mathrm df:L_J\to L_{J'}$ are $k$-linear, and
$$f(E_{J,R}(u))=E_{J',R}((\mathrm df\otimes1)(u)).$$
For a closed subgroup inclusion $i:B\hookrightarrow J$ [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup], $\mathrm di$ is injective and the preceding identity identifies $E_{B,R}(L_B\otimes_k R)$ with
$$B(R[\delta])\cap\ker J(p_R)\subseteq J(R[\delta]).$$
Finally there is a homomorphism of $k$-group schemes $\operatorname{Ad}_J:J\to\operatorname{GL}(L_J)$, where $\operatorname{GL}(L_J)(R)$ is the group of invertible $R$-linear maps of $L_J\otimes_k R$, characterized for every $R$, $j\in J(R)$ and $u\in L_J\otimes_k R$ by
$$jE_{J,R}(u)j^{-1}=E_{J,R}(\operatorname{Ad}_J(j)u).$$
Here $j$ in $J(R[\delta])$ is its image under $R\hookrightarrow R[\delta]$. For every homomorphism $f:J\to J'$, one has
$$(\mathrm df\otimes1)(\operatorname{Ad}_J(j)u)=\operatorname{Ad}_{J'}(f(j))((\mathrm df\otimes1)(u)).$$
No smoothness, reducedness, connectedness or characteristic-zero hypothesis is imposed.

source.place: 10.6 (augmentation cotangent dual), 10.11 (addition and scaling), 10.14 (subgroups), 10.18–10.21 (scalar-extended infinitesimal points and adjoint action), printed pp.188–193. The augmentation-ideal computation of 10.19 works for every commutative k-algebra R, not just finitely generated ones.

proof.text: Write $J=\operatorname{Spec}A$ and let $\epsilon:A\to k$, $\Delta:A\to A\otimes_k A$, and $S:A\to A$ be the counit, coproduct and antipode. The coordinate Hopf node supplies these maps and their identities, with multiplication of points given by $(x y)(a)=\sum x(a_{(1)})y(a_{(2)})$. Apply the affine-pair criterion for locally finite type to the structure morphism, with affine opens $J$ and $\operatorname{Spec}k$. Thus $A$ has finitely many algebra generators $c_1,\ldots,c_m$. Put $I=\ker\epsilon$ and $M=I/I^2$. In tensor expressions, scalar counit values are understood via the structure map into the target algebra.

source.place: 10.6 and 10.19, printed pp.188,192; Hopf coordinates of Chapter 3; finite generation also Stacks Tag 01T2, lemma-locally-finite-type-characterize

proof.text: The unit splits $\epsilon$, so every $a\in A$ is uniquely $\epsilon(a)1+b$ with $b\in I$. Modulo $I^2$ the product of $(c,x)$ and $(c',x')$ is $(cc',cx'+c'x)$; hence $A/I^2=k\oplus M$ as an augmented square-zero algebra. The elements $b_i=c_i-\epsilon(c_i)$ generate $I$: for any polynomial $P$, the difference $P(c_1,\ldots,c_m)-P(\epsilon(c_1),\ldots,\epsilon(c_m))$ is a sum of multiples of the $b_i$, by subtracting one variable at a time. Modulo $I^2$ each multiplier may be replaced by its counit. Therefore the classes $\bar b_i$ span $M$ over $k$, so $M$ is finite-dimensional. Apply the finite linear dual node with $V=W=M$ and $f=1_M$ to conclude that $M^*=\operatorname{Hom}_k(M,k)$ is finite-dimensional.

source.place: 10.6, formula (56), printed p.188; 10.19, printed p.192; split augmentation sequence 3.22

proof.text: For any commutative $k$-algebra $R$, an element $x$ of the kernel in the statement is an algebra map $A\to R[\delta]$ with reduction $\epsilon_R$. Write it uniquely as $x(a)=\epsilon(a)+\delta d(a)$. Multiplicativity says exactly $d(ab)=\epsilon(a)d(b)+\epsilon(b)d(a)$, with $d$ $k$-linear and zero on $k$. Thus $d(I^2)=0$, and restriction determines $\lambda\in\operatorname{Hom}_k(M,R)$. Conversely, for such $\lambda$, put $d_\lambda(a)=\lambda(\overline{a-\epsilon(a)})$. The product formula of step 2 shows that $\epsilon+\delta d_\lambda$ is a unital algebra map. These two constructions are inverse, including for the zero ring $R$. This proves a canonical bijection between the kernel and $\operatorname{Hom}_k(M,R)$.

source.place: 10.6 and 10.19, printed pp.188,192; coefficient calculation also Proposition 10.28, printed p.195

proof.text: For $R=k$, the kernel is the dual-number tangent set at $e$, by its definition. Its identification with $M^*$ from step 3 is linear for the tangent operations specified in that definition: the common lift of two tangent maps to the algebra with basis $1,\delta_1,\delta_2$ has formula $a\mapsto\epsilon(a)+\delta_1d_1(a)+\delta_2d_2(a)$; sending both variables to $\delta$ adds the coefficients. Sending $\delta$ to $t\delta$ multiplies the coefficient by $t$. We consequently identify $L_J$ linearly with $M^*$, and step 2 proves its finite dimension. For a group homomorphism $f:J\to J'$, composition of tangent maps is the tangent map of the definition, so in these coordinates it is precomposition by $f^*:A'\to A$ on coefficient maps, which is $k$-linear.

source.place: 10.6 and 10.11, printed pp.188–189; 10.19, formula (59), printed p.192

proof.text:
The tensor–Hom node, specialized to the finite $k$-module $M$, to $P=R$ and $Q=k$, gives the isomorphism $R\otimes_k M^*\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_k(M,R\otimes_k k)$. Its projectivity hypothesis holds: remove dependent vectors from the finite spanning list of step 2 to obtain a basis; a linear map out of $M$ lifts through any surjection by choosing lifts of its finitely many basis images, which is the lifting characterization of projectivity. Tensor symmetry and the unit identification $R\otimes_k k\simeq R$ give
$$\beta_R:L_J\otimes_k R\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Hom}_k(M,R),\qquad \beta_R(v\otimes r)(z)=r\,v(z).$$
The symmetry and unit identifications are inverse on pure tensors, by the tensor universal property. This is $R$-linear for the scalar-extension module structure. Define $E_{J,R}(u)$ to be the map $a\mapsto\epsilon(a)+\delta\beta_R(u)(\overline{a-\epsilon(a)})$ of step 3. It is a bijection and for $R=k$ is precisely the tangent identification of step 4.

source.place: 10.19, printed p.192: the last tensor–dual identification, made explicit by finite-projective tensor–Hom

proof.text:
For $x_u=E_{J,R}(u)$ and $x_v=E_{J,R}(v)$, write their coefficient maps as $d_u,d_v$. Multiplying their values against $\Delta(a)$ gives
$$(x_u x_v)(a)=\epsilon(a)+\delta\sum\bigl(\epsilon(a_{(1)})d_v(a_{(2)})+d_u(a_{(1)})\epsilon(a_{(2)})\bigr)=\epsilon(a)+\delta(d_u(a)+d_v(a)).$$
Here the term in $\delta^2$ vanishes and the two counit identities give the last equality. By the formula for $\beta_R$, this is $E_{J,R}(u+v)$. The zero coefficient map is the identity point. Taking $v=-u$ gives the asserted inverse formula. Applying $\delta\mapsto a\delta$ for $a\in R$ replaces $d_u$ by $a d_u$, which is $\beta_R(au)$, and proves the scaling assertion.

source.place: 10.11, printed p.189; scalar-extended version in 10.19, printed p.192

proof.text: For a $k$-algebra homomorphism $h:R\to R'$, applying $h$ to coefficients sends $\beta_R(v\otimes r)(z)=r v(z)$ to $h(r)v(z)$, exactly the formula for $\beta_{R'}((1\otimes h)(v\otimes r))$. Since pure tensors span, the same holds for every $u$, and the formula defining $E$ proves naturality in $R$. For $f:J\to J'$, its pullback $f^*:A'\to A$ preserves counits and sends $I'$ into $I$ and $(I')^2$ into $I^2$. Thus the coefficient of $f(E_{J,R}(u))$ is $d_u\circ f^*$. On $v\otimes r$ this is the coefficient of $(\mathrm df(v))\otimes r$ by step 4; tensor linearity gives $f(E_{J,R}(u))=E_{J',R}((\mathrm df\otimes1)u)$.

For a closed subgroup $i:B\hookrightarrow J$, the affine closed-immersion description gives $B=\operatorname{Spec}(A/K)$; the images of the $c_i$ generate $A/K$, so steps 2–5 apply to this coordinate algebra and define $L_B$ and $E_{B,R}$ directly. Its maps on points are injective by the subgroup definition. In particular the map on tangent sets at $R=k$ is injective, hence $\mathrm di$ is injective. Its image on scalar extension remains injective: extend a basis of the image of $\mathrm di$ to a basis of $L_J$ and obtain a linear left inverse; tensor that left inverse with $R$. If $b\in B(R[\delta])$ lies in the kernel after inclusion into $J$, then $i(p_R(b))=e_J$. Injectivity of $B(R)\to J(R)$ implies $p_R(b)=e_B$. Conversely any such $b$ is in that intersection. Apply step 7 and the two $E$ bijections to identify this intersection with the asserted image of $L_B\otimes_k R$.

source.place: 10.14, printed p.190; scalar extension as in 10.19, printed p.192

proof.text:
For $j\in J(R)$, conjugation by its constant lift preserves the kernel since $p_R$ is a group homomorphism. Use the iterated coproduct $\sum a_{(1)}\otimes a_{(2)}\otimes a_{(3)}$ and the inverse point $j\circ S$. The coefficient of $j E_{J,R}(u)j^{-1}$ is
$$D_j(d_u)(a)=\sum j(a_{(1)})\,d_u(a_{(2)})\,j(S(a_{(3)})).$$
This follows by multiplying the three values; the middle factor is the only one with a $\delta$ term. Because the result is a kernel point, step 3 identifies its coefficient with a functional on $M$. The displayed formula is $R$-linear in $d_u$. Conjugation by $j^{-1}$ is its inverse. Hence $C_R(j)=\beta_R^{-1}D_j\beta_R$ is an invertible $R$-linear map of $L_J\otimes_k R$. For $h:R\to R'$, the displayed finite sum is preserved by applying $h$, and the formula for $\beta$ in step 7 proves naturality of $C_R(j)$ in $R$.

source.place: 10.20–10.21, printed pp.192–193; explicit coordinate verification of R-linearity

proof.text: Put $n=\dim L_J$. If $n>0$, choose a basis. Let $j_{\rm univ}\in J(A)$ be the point corresponding to $1_A:A\to A$. The matrix $K$ of $C_A(j_{\rm univ})$ lies in $\operatorname{GL}_n(A)$ by step 9, and its inverse is the matrix obtained from $j_{\rm univ}^{-1}$. The general-linear-group node therefore supplies a morphism $\operatorname{Spec}A\to\operatorname{GL}_n$; explicitly its pullback sends $x_{rs}$ to $K_{rs}$ and $\det^{-1}$ to $(\det K)^{-1}$. For every point $j:A\to R$, naturality in step 9 says that the image matrix is $j(K)$, precisely $C_R(j)$. Transporting the basis identifies the target with $\operatorname{GL}(L_J)$. For $n=0$, every $L_J\otimes_k R$ is zero and has exactly one automorphism; this functor is represented by the trivial group $\operatorname{Spec}k$. The resulting morphism has the same characterization. Thus both cases produce a morphism inducing all $C_R$.

source.place: 10.20, printed p.192; algebraicity verified by the universal affine point and the determinant localization

proof.text: Conjugation satisfies $c_{j_1j_2}=c_{j_1}\circ c_{j_2}$ and $c_e=1$. Transport through the $E$ bijections gives $C_R(j_1j_2)=C_R(j_1)C_R(j_2)$ and $C_R(e)=1$ for every $R$. Apply full faithfulness of Yoneda on the category of affine $k$-schemes to the representing affine schemes: these equalities on all affine points give the multiplication and unit diagrams for the morphism of step 10. It is therefore a group-scheme homomorphism $\operatorname{Ad}_J$. The same full faithfulness shows uniqueness from its conjugation characterization and independence of the basis in step 10. The hypothesis of the cited Yoneda node is met because both $J$ and the constructed $\operatorname{GL}(L_J)$ are affine $k$-schemes and their point functors are the representables on that category.

source.place: 10.20–10.21, printed pp.192–193; Stacks Tag 001P, lemma-yoneda, for passage from affine points to morphisms

proof.text:
Finally, apply a group homomorphism $f:J\to J'$ to $jE_{J,R}(u)j^{-1}$. The group law gives $f(j)f(E_{J,R}(u))f(j)^{-1}$. By step 7 and the definition of $\operatorname{Ad}$, the two expressions are respectively
$$E_{J',R}((\mathrm df\otimes1)(\operatorname{Ad}_J(j)u)),\qquad E_{J',R}(\operatorname{Ad}_{J'}(f(j))((\mathrm df\otimes1)u)).$$
The injectivity of $E_{J',R}$ proves the final equivariance identity. Every calculation used only the square-zero relation, finite generation for $M$, and Hopf identities, so it imposed none of the extra hypotheses excluded by the statement.
